summary: For ages 9-10, build representation fluency so a child moves between real situations, bar models, number lines, multi-digit multiplication, and the fraction-decimal-percentage trio while explaining the connections and keeping each symbol tied to the quantity it names. The signature demand is seeing 0.35, 35/100 and 35% as ONE quantity shown three ways, located on a single representation (a hundredths grid, or one number line with fractions above and decimals/percents below) so equivalence is a fact of magnitude, not three separate conversion rules. Percentage is the fresh hazard: 'per cent' means 'parts per hundred', and a child who has not internalised that reads 35% as the bare number 35 or an unmoored decimal. Scaling problems (bar model mapped to a multiplication equation) and reading quantities off a line graph into an equation round out the level; the recurring failure is grabbing visible numbers without asking what quantity each representation actually shows.
misconceptions: Treats 0.35, 35/100 and 35% as three different things rather than one magnitude shown three ways
Does not hold 'per cent = parts per hundred', so reads 35% as the number 35 (or a decimal with no meaning)
Grabs both readings off a line graph and adds them instead of asking which quantity and which operation the situation needs
Reads a bar/area model as a separate procedure from the multiplication equation it represents

activities.title: One quantity, three costumes: the linked hundredths grid
steps: Shade 35 of 100 squares on a hundredths grid and read off the three labels that name the same shaded region: 35/100, 0.35 and 35%.
Change the shading to a different amount (e.g. 8 squares) and state the fraction, decimal and percentage, explaining why all three must still match the shaded area.
Place the same quantity at a single point on one number line that carries fractions above and decimals/percentages below.
Answer the direct challenge: 'Is 0.35 the same as 35%, or is one bigger?' and justify using the shaded area and the per-hundred meaning, not '35 is bigger than nought-point-something'.
Say aloud what the % symbol means ('parts per hundred') and what the quantity is 35% OF.
activities.insight: 0.35, 35/100 and 35% were never three numbers to convert between; they are one magnitude shown three ways, and 'per cent' means parts per hundred.

activities.title: Scaling bar mapped to a multiplication equation
steps: Represent a scaling situation (e.g. a recipe for 4 scaled to 12) as a bar model showing the equal parts.
Write the multiplication equation that matches the bar (here 4×3=12, a scale of ×3), and point to which part of the bar each number in the equation refers to.
If the scale changes, adjust the bar and update the equation together, explaining why the multiplier changes.
State what quantity each number represents before computing.
activities.insight: A bar model and a multiplication equation describe the same multiplicative/scaling structure; the bar and the symbols are two views of one relationship.

activities.title: Reading a line graph for meaning before choosing an operation
steps: On a line graph, name what quantity each point/reading represents before doing any arithmetic.
For a question asking the change or difference between two readings, state which operation the situation needs and why.
Translate the reading into an equation (e.g. a subtraction for a difference) and compute.
Explain why adding the two readings would not give the change.
activities.insight: Choose the operation from what the situation asks and what each reading means, not by grabbing whichever visible numbers are present.

activities.title: Argue it out: defend equivalence against a doubter
steps: Respond to a partner who claims '35% must be bigger than 0.35 — 35 versus nought-point-something!' by proving sameness on the grid.
Explain in your own words why 35/100, 0.35 and 35% are the same proportion.
When the partner reads a line graph aloud and proposes adding two values to find a change, say whether that is right and correct it, giving your reasoning.
activities.insight: Being able to explain and defend why the three forms are one quantity, and why an operation does or doesn't fit, shows understanding beyond rote conversion.

checkQuestion: On a hundred-square, 35 squares are shaded. One classmate says 'that shows 35/100', another says 'no, it's 0.35', another says 'it's 35%'. Who is right? Explain how these three are related, and show me on the grid. Then tell me: is 35% a bigger amount than 0.35, or the same?
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child recognising all three name the SAME shaded quantity (thirty-five hundredths), explaining per cent as parts per hundred, and stating that 35% and 0.35 are the same amount — not that one is larger because '35 > 0.35'.
